pillar_reactions.evidence: Presented as the most efficient way to train, three to four days a week, 30-45 minute sessions, first month devoted to mastering form, with mobility framed as preventing the aches and sleep disruption he had described. He asked practical adoption questions ('How long are the workouts for usually?', 'is this all like on an app or something?', 'it has videos and everything showing you how to do the work?') and then tied it to his own life unprompted: 'It's time efficient. It's going to give me the results. It's going to keep me athletic and be able to move and stuff and hang out with my kids and go out.'

He asked for it directly — 'And then how about the diet? What type of diet do you guys recommend on this kind of program?' — and received the standard eat-for-health answer: red meat, eggs, dairy, fruit, vegetables, sweet potato, micronutrients over macros, plus fasting. He raised no objection and asked no follow-up, despite currently eating wheat bread, multigrain sandwiches, rice, tortillas and pre-made protein shakes, all of which sit outside what was described. The mismatch was never surfaced by either party.

Presented as 24/7 access to Trevor, high-communication video feedback through the first month, and education so he does not need coaching forever. The prospect acknowledged it flatly — 'Okay', 'And all of the above' — without questions and without connecting it to a problem of his own. Reasonable, since accountability is the one thing he has demonstrably not lacked: he has trained four days a week for eighteen months unaided.

anchors.raw: I've been going to the gym for about a year and a half now. I lost about 60 pounds. So I lost a big chunk of fat and I gained some muscle... I think I look decent for the amount of work I put in in a year and a half.
anchors.note: The strongest structural anchor here: he has already produced a large result on his own, for the price of a gym membership. Any $6,000-$9,000 case has to be made against a method that is visibly working for him. The rep did not address it — he congratulated the result ('I'm glad that you're happy with the progress') rather than reframing the plateau on the last of the abdominal fat, which is the one place the current method has stalled.

anchors.raw: So I'm always in a rush to go to the gyms, which sucks.
anchors.note: His reference cost for fitness is a monthly gym membership plus time. The rep argued the time contrast well and never touched the cost contrast, so the price landed against a subscription frame.

anchors.raw: I'll probably go with the $9,000 one, but I've to talk to her since it's a large investment.
anchors.note: On hearing both tiers he moved up rather than down, unprompted and without any consequence frame having been run. Price is functioning as a quality signal for this prospect, which is the defining marker of the optimizer profile and is the strongest supportive signal in the batch.

unmet_demand.want: A clear answer on whether calisthenics is programmed alongside the kettlebell work — he asked directly and specifically
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The question 'Is it all kettlebell work? Are you going to do calisthenics as well?' was answered with the three-pillar description, which does not include calisthenics. It surfaced only later and only as something he would be educated on: 'educate you on the calisthenics side of it.' The programme does combine kettlebells and calisthenics, as this rep stated plainly on another call, so this is a communication failure rather than a product limitation.

unmet_demand.want: Reassurance that a kettlebell programme will finish the job on the last of his abdominal fat, after eighteen months of self-directed work stalled there
unmet_demand.why_unmet: This is his actual buying trigger and it was never addressed. The rep said the nutrition would be 'optimized to get shredded, right? Because it's a different game' and moved on. No explanation of why his current approach has plateaued or what specifically would change.
